title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
hookLine: he can't hold back: I am your brother, don't be distressed, God sent me ahead

cards: Judah has just finished speaking. The room is silent: Egyptian servants by the walls, eleven brothers fallen on the ground, an old father far away.
And the governor, who has held his face still through three days of custody, a feast, a planted cup and Judah's whole plea, can't hold it anymore.
In the King James Bible: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me." The servants file out. The door closes.
Now there's only family in the room.

teach.b: He weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it outside, and the news reaches Pharaoh's house. Then he says it: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?"

In Hebrew, I am Joseph is just two words, and he has waited years to say them. The brothers can't answer; they are troubled at his presence, the text says. The boy they threw in a pit holds their lives in his hand.
So he says, come near to me, and they come closer.

teach.h: I AM JOSEPH, WHOM YE SOLD.
teach.b: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. He names it.
And before anyone can say sorry: "Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life."

He tells the truth about the wrong, and in the same breath tells them not to be crushed by it. He has had years to decide what this story means, and he has decided God was in it, keeping people alive.
That doesn't make what they did good. It means the story isn't only about what they did. He falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps, and kisses all his brothers.
Then a quiet line that reaches back to the beginning: "after that his brethren talked with him."
Once they could not speak peaceably unto him. Now they talk.
Some Christian readers hear in this a picture of the forgiveness they believe God offers: the one who was wronged moves first, names the wrong, and draws people near.

how: Christians often read Joseph's words to his brothers as a picture of forgiveness, and preachers set them beside Jesus's teaching to forgive from the heart (Matthew 18:35).

games.q: you're Joseph. your brothers are on their knees, terrified, unable to answer. you've just told them who you are. what do you do?
o: remind them of everything they did, in detail.
say come near, name the wrong, and tell them not to be grieved.
send them home and never see them again.
games.why: he draws them close, says whom ye sold into Egypt, then: be not grieved, God sent me before you to preserve life.

practice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you and hasn't apologized, maybe never will. Joseph didn't pretend; he said, you sold me, so name what they did honestly in your own mind, then, if you can, loosen your grip on it, even a little.
Forgiving doesn't mean trusting again right away, and if you pray, you can ask for help with it.

wordCard.voice: Joseph. Hebrew for may he add: the name he reveals to his brothers at last, calling himself their brother despite what they did.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am Joseph. Joseph's name is tied in Genesis 30 to the hope that God would add another son.

carryVoice: Your line: I am your brother. He named the wrong, and still called them brothers. Day three hundred seventy-three, done.
